scenario: You plan to move older blobs to the Archive tier, but the option isn't available on your storage account. The account uses ZRS. Why?

options.text: Archive isn't supported with ZRS redundancy.

options.note: Archive is a Standard-only tier.
Not a requirement.

options.text: Archive is only available for append blobs.
options.note: Archive applies to block blobs.

explanation: The Archive tier is only supported for accounts that use LRS, GRS or RA-GRS redundancy. Accounts with ZRS, GZRS or RA-GZRS can use Hot, Cool and Cold, but not Archive. To archive data from a ZRS account, you'd need to change its redundancy or copy the data to an account that supports Archive.

refs.title: Access tiers for blob data: Archive access tier

scenario: You delete a blob that was moved to the Cool tier 10 days ago. What charge applies?

options.text: None; Cool has no minimum retention.
options.note: Cool has a minimum retention period.

options.text: An early deletion charge for 20 days
An early deletion charge for 170 days
options.note: 180 days is the Archive minimum.
Rehydration applies to Archive only.

explanation: Each cooler tier has a minimum storage period: 30 days for Cool, 90 days for Cold and 180 days for Archive. Deleting or re-tiering a blob before then adds a prorated early deletion charge for the remaining days. A blob in Cool for 10 days is charged for the remaining 20.

refs.title: Access tiers for blob data: Summary of access tier options

scenario: Regulations require that audit logs in a container can't be modified or deleted by anyone, including admins, for 7 years. What should you configure?

options.text: Blob soft delete with a 7-year retention.
options.note: Soft delete allows deletion and permanent purge after retention; it doesn't prevent changes.

options.text: A CanNotDelete lock on the storage account
options.note: Locks protect the account resource, not the blob data, and can be removed.
Versions can still be deleted.

explanation: Immutable storage keeps blobs in a write-once, read-many (WORM) state. With a time-based retention policy of 7 years that's been locked, nobody, including account admins, can modify or delete the blobs until retention ends, and the period can only be extended. Soft delete and resource locks don't stop data being overwritten or deleted.

refs.title: Immutable Storage for Blob Data Overview
Immutable Storage for Blob Data Overview: Time-based retention policies

scenario: Legal counsel needs blobs related to an ongoing lawsuit kept unchanged until the case ends, with no known end date. Which immutability option fits?

options.text: A time-based retention policy of 10 years.
options.note: There's no known end date, and retention can't be shortened once locked.

options.text: A legal hold on the container or blob versions.
Changing the blobs to the Archive tier.
options.note: Archive doesn't prevent deletion.
Doesn't make data immutable.

explanation: A legal hold keeps data immutable until the hold is explicitly cleared, with no retention period to set. That makes it the right choice when the end date is unknown, such as during litigation. Each hold is identified by a tag, for example a case ID, and data stays protected while any hold remains.

refs.title: Immutable Storage for Blob Data Overview: Legal holds

scenario: You want to be able to restore an entire container of block blobs to its state at a specific time in the past 7 days. Which feature should you enable?

options.note: Recovers deleted containers, not earlier states of blobs.
For file shares, not blobs.
Copies blobs to another account; no rollback.

explanation: Point-in-time restore rolls block blobs in a container (or a range of blobs) back to their state at an earlier time. It requires blob versioning, change feed and blob soft delete, and the restore window must be shorter than the soft delete retention. Container soft delete only recovers a deleted container; it can't undo changes to blobs.

refs.title: Point-in-time restore for block blobs

scenario: A container was deleted by mistake. Which feature lets you recover it with its blobs, if it was enabled beforehand?

options.note: Doesn't recover a deleted container.
Versions are deleted along with the container.
The deletion replicates to the secondary.

explanation: Container soft delete keeps a deleted container and all its blobs for a retention period you set (1 to 365 days), so you can restore it. It has to be enabled before the deletion. Blob soft delete and versioning protect individual blobs, but not a deleted container.

refs.title: Soft Delete for Containers in Azure Storage

scenario: Someone deletes an Azure file share. How can you recover it?

options.text: Undelete it from share soft delete.

options.note: Versioning applies to blobs, not file shares.

options.text: Rehydrate it from the Archive tier.
options.note: File shares don't use the Archive tier.

options.text: It can't be recovered under any circumstances.
options.note: Soft delete for shares is enabled by default on new accounts.

explanation: Soft delete for Azure file shares keeps a deleted share, including its share snapshots, for the retention period (7 days by default, up to 365), and you can undelete it from the portal, PowerShell or the CLI. It's on by default for new storage accounts. Blob features such as versioning don't apply to file shares.

refs.title: Azure File Share Soft Delete

scenario: Users need to recover earlier versions of individual files in an Azure file share from the Previous Versions tab in Windows. What should you use?

options.text: Blob versioning on the storage account
options.note: Applies to blob storage only.
Moves or deletes blobs; doesn't apply to file shares.
Blob-only and not for file versions.

explanation: Share snapshots are read-only, point-in-time copies of an Azure file share. Windows clients see them on the Previous Versions tab, so users can restore individual files or folders themselves. Azure Backup for Azure Files can schedule and retain these snapshots automatically.

refs.title: Use Azure Files Share Snapshots

scenario: Domain-joined Windows clients must access an Azure file share using their on-premises AD DS credentials, with existing NTFS permissions applying. What should you configure?

options.text: The storage account key saved in each client's Credential Manager
options.note: Key-based access gives full share access and ignores per-user permissions.

options.text: A SAS token for each user.
options.note: SMB access doesn't use SAS tokens.
Not supported for Azure Files and insecure.

explanation: With identity-based authentication over on-premises AD DS, domain-joined clients use Kerberos with their own AD credentials to access the share, with no storage key on the client. Share-level access is granted with Azure RBAC roles, and the existing NTFS ACLs then control files and folders. Microsoft Entra Domain Services and Microsoft Entra Kerberos are the other supported identity sources.

refs.title: Azure Files Identity-Based Authentication
Enable AD DS Authentication for Azure Files

scenario: Users authenticate to an Azure file share with their AD identities. A group needs read, write and delete access to files at the share level, but not the ability to change NTFS permissions. Which role should you assign?

options.text: Storage File Data SMB Share Reader
options.note: Read-only.

options.text: Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor
Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor
options.note: Also lets users modify NTFS permissions.
A management-plane role that doesn't grant SMB data access.

explanation: Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor grants read, write and delete access to files over SMB. It doesn't allow changing NTFS permissions; that needs SMB Share Elevated Contributor. Storage File Data SMB Share Reader is read-only, and Storage Account Contributor is a control-plane role that doesn't give file access.

refs.title: Assign Share-Level Permissions for Azure Files

scenario: A remote user can't map an Azure file share from home over SMB, but it works from the office. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The user's ISP or home router blocks outbound TCP port 445.
Azure Files only works from inside Azure.
options.note: SMB works from on-premises and the internet when port 445 is open.

options.text: The share is in the Hot tier.
options.note: The tier doesn't affect connectivity.

options.text: SMB 3.x doesn't support encryption over the internet.
options.note: SMB 3.x encrypts in transit, which is why internet access is allowed.

explanation: SMB uses TCP port 445, and many ISPs and home routers block outbound 445, so the share works from the office but not from home. Workarounds include a point-to-site VPN, ExpressRoute, Azure File Sync to a local server, or SMB over QUIC. Azure Files itself is reachable from anywhere SMB 3.x can get through.

refs.title: Troubleshoot Azure Files SMB connectivity and access issues

scenario: Branch file servers sync with an Azure file share using Azure File Sync, but local disk space is running out. Infrequently used files should stay available but only use space in Azure. What should you enable?

options.text: Cloud tiering on the server endpoint
Lifecycle management on the storage account
options.note: Lifecycle rules apply to blobs, not File Sync servers.

options.text: Blob versioning on the storage account
options.note: Not related to File Sync.
Doesn't free local space.

explanation: Cloud tiering on an Azure File Sync server endpoint keeps frequently used files cached on the local server and replaces rarely used ones with pointers. Tiered files still appear in their folders and are recalled from Azure when someone opens them. A volume free-space policy (and an optional date policy) decides what gets tiered.

refs.title: Understand Azure File Sync Cloud Tiering

scenario: You create an Azure File Sync sync group. How many cloud endpoints can the sync group contain?

options.note: Only one cloud endpoint is allowed.
Only one cloud endpoint is allowed.

options.text: None; only server endpoints are used
options.note: Every sync group needs a cloud endpoint (an Azure file share).

explanation: A sync group defines one sync topology: exactly one cloud endpoint (an Azure file share) and one or more server endpoints (paths on registered servers). To sync another file share, you create another sync group. A server can be registered to only one Storage Sync Service at a time.

refs.title: Plan an Azure File Sync deployment

scenario: You need to transfer 70 TB of data from an office with a slow internet connection to Azure Blob storage within two weeks. What should you use?

options.note: Too slow over a constrained link.
Also limited by the slow link.
Syncs over the network and isn't meant for bulk one-time loads.

explanation: Azure Data Box is a rugged appliance with about 80 TB of usable capacity. Microsoft ships it to you, you copy the data locally, and Microsoft uploads it to your storage account in the Azure datacenter, so the slow internet link doesn't matter. 70 TB over a slow connection wouldn't finish in two weeks.

refs.title: Microsoft Azure Data Box overview

scenario: You want storage account encryption to use keys that your organization controls and can revoke. What must the Key Vault have enabled to store the customer-managed key?

options.text: Public network access from all networks
options.note: Not required; firewalls with trusted services work.
Standard vaults work; HSM-backed keys are optional.
Either access model works.

explanation: Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage must be in a Key Vault or Managed HSM that has both soft delete and purge protection enabled, so the key can't be permanently deleted by mistake, leaving the data unreadable. The storage account reads the key through a managed identity with permission on the vault.

refs.title: Customer-managed keys for account encryption

scenario: Compliance requires a second layer of encryption for data at rest in a new storage account, using a different algorithm and key. When must this be enabled?

options.text: Any time after creation from the Encryption blade.
options.note: Infrastructure encryption can't be enabled on an existing account.
Not related to performance tier.
Works with Microsoft-managed keys too.

explanation: Infrastructure encryption adds a second layer of encryption at the infrastructure level, using a different algorithm and key, on top of the default service-level encryption. It can only be enabled when you create the storage account, or on an encryption scope when you create the scope; it can't be turned on later.

refs.title: Enable infrastructure encryption for double encryption of data

scenario: An app signs SAS tokens with Microsoft Entra credentials instead of the account key, so access can be revoked without rotating keys and is tied to an identity. Which SAS type is this?

options.note: Signed with the account key.
Signed with the account key.
A service SAS associated with a policy; still key-signed.

explanation: A user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key obtained with Microsoft Entra credentials, not with the account key. Access is tied to an identity and its RBAC permissions, and you can revoke it by revoking the delegation keys without touching the account keys. It's supported for Blob storage and Data Lake Storage.

refs.title: Create a user delegation SAS
Grant limited access to data with shared access signatures (SAS): Types of shared access signatures

scenario: Security policy requires that all requests to a storage account be authorized with Microsoft Entra ID; access keys and key-signed SAS tokens must stop working. What should you configure?

options.note: Rotation only replaces keys; they still work.
Enforces HTTPS, not the authorization method.
Locks affect management operations, not data authorization.

explanation: Setting Allow storage account key access to Disabled blocks Shared Key authorization. Requests signed with the account keys, including account and service SAS tokens signed with those keys, are rejected. Microsoft Entra ID (OAuth) and user delegation SAS keep working. Check that every app and tool can use Entra authorization first.

refs.title: Prevent authorization with Shared Key

scenario: You need to rotate storage account keys without downtime for apps that use them. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Regenerate both keys at the same time during a maintenance window
options.note: Breaks every app immediately.

options.text: Switch apps to key2, regenerate key1, then repeat
Delete the storage account and recreate it.
options.note: Destroys data.
Unrelated to keys.

explanation: Every storage account has two access keys so you can rotate them without downtime. Point all apps at key2, regenerate key1, move the apps back to key1, then regenerate key2. Better still, keep keys in Key Vault with automatic rotation, or avoid keys entirely with managed identities and Entra authorization.

refs.title: Manage account access keys

scenario: The storage account firewall allows only selected networks. Azure Backup and Azure Monitor diagnostic logs must still be able to write to the account. What should you enable?

options.note: Opens data to the public.

options.text: A service endpoint for each Azure region the services run in
options.note: Not possible and not needed.
Defeats the purpose of the firewall.

explanation: When the storage firewall allows only selected networks, the Allow trusted Microsoft services exception lets specific Azure services, such as Azure Backup, Azure Monitor diagnostic logs, Event Grid and Site Recovery, still reach the account. Resource instance rules are a narrower alternative that allow specific resource instances.

refs.title: Trusted Azure services for Azure Storage network security

scenario: You need to host a static marketing website (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) directly from a storage account. Where must the files be uploaded after you enable static website hosting?

options.note: The service only serves from $web.
Static websites are served from blob storage.

options.text: The root of the storage account
options.note: Files must be in the $web container.

explanation: Enabling static website hosting creates a container named $web and a web endpoint such as https://name.z13.web.core.windows.net. Files you upload to $web are served at that endpoint. You also set an index document and, optionally, a 404 error document.

refs.title: Static website hosting in Azure Storage

scenario: An app reads data from an RA-GRS storage account. The primary region is unavailable. Which endpoint should the app use to keep reading data?

options.note: Not a valid endpoint.
The suffix is appended to the account name, not prefixed.

options.text: Reading isn't possible until a failover
options.note: RA-GRS provides read access to the secondary at all times.

explanation: With read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS or RA-GZRS), the secondary region has a read-only endpoint: the account name plus -secondary, for example account-secondary.blob.core.windows.net. Apps can keep reading from it while the primary is down. Writes still need the primary region or a failover.

refs.title: Use geo-redundancy to design highly available applications
Data redundancy: Read access to data in the secondary region

scenario: You need to copy 2 TB of blobs from one storage account to another in a different region as fast as possible, without the data passing through your workstation. What should you do?

options.text: Download with Storage Explorer, then upload.
options.note: Data travels through your machine.

options.text: Run azcopy copy between the two account URLs.

options.note: File Sync works with file shares and servers.
Uploads from your machine only.

explanation: azcopy copy between two storage account URLs runs a server-to-server copy (using Put Block From URL), so the data moves directly between the accounts inside Azure and never passes through your workstation. That's fast even across regions. Downloading and re-uploading with Storage Explorer would send all 2 TB through your machine twice.

refs.title: Copy blobs between Azure storage accounts with AzCopy v10

scenario: You want to find blobs across containers by custom attributes such as project=apollo and status=final, and use those attributes in lifecycle rules. What should you use?

options.note: Metadata isn't indexed for querying across containers.

options.text: Resource tags on the storage account
options.note: Apply to the account, not individual blobs.
Not queryable as key-value pairs.

explanation: Blob index tags are key-value attributes on individual blobs that Azure indexes, so you can query them across every container with Find Blobs by Tags (for example project = 'apollo' AND status = 'final'). Lifecycle management rules can filter on them too. Container metadata isn't indexed or searchable this way.

refs.title: Manage and find Azure Blob data with blob index tags

scenario: Which operation is allowed while a storage account has a CanNotDelete lock?

options.note: Blocked by the lock.

options.text: Uploading and deleting blobs inside containers
Deleting the resource group that contains it
options.note: Blocked because of the locked resource.

options.text: Removing the lock without the right permissions
options.note: Requires Owner or User Access Administrator.

explanation: Resource locks apply to the management plane, meaning operations on the storage account resource itself, such as deleting it or its resource group. Data-plane operations, such as uploading, overwriting or deleting blobs, aren't affected. To protect the data itself, use soft delete, versioning or immutability policies.

refs.title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure

scenario: You configure a lifecycle rule to delete blobs 90 days after creation, but some blobs are still there after 100 days. Which is a possible explanation?

options.text: New or changed policies can take up to 24 hours to take effect
Lifecycle rules only run on Premium block blob accounts
options.note: They work on GPv2, Blob storage and Premium block blob accounts.
No such requirement.

options.text: Delete isn't a supported lifecycle action.
options.note: Delete is supported.

explanation: After you create or change a lifecycle management policy, it can take up to 24 hours before it takes effect. After that, each run can take a while on accounts with many blobs. Also check the rule's filters (prefix, blob type, index tags) and whether the blobs are under an immutability policy or legal hold, which blocks deletion.

refs.title: Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management overview: Policy execution

scenario: You need to convert an existing storage account from LRS to GRS. What is true?

options.text: Change the redundancy setting in place
Create a new GRS account and copy the data with AzCopy
options.note: Not required for LRS to GRS; the setting can be changed in place.

options.text: GRS is only available for Premium accounts.
options.note: GRS is a Standard-tier option.

options.text: Conversion requires deleting all blobs first.
options.note: Data stays in place.

explanation: You can change between LRS, GRS and RA-GRS in place on the storage account's Redundancy setting, with no data copy and no downtime. Azure then starts replicating to the secondary region in the background. Changes that add zone redundancy (to ZRS or GZRS) use a conversion process instead.

refs.title: Change how a storage account is replicated

scenario: You deploy an ARM template to rg-web using Complete mode. The resource group contains a storage account that isn't defined in the template. What happens to it?

options.note: That's Incremental mode behavior.

options.text: The deployment fails with a validation error.
options.note: Complete mode doesn't fail because of extra resources.

options.text: It's moved to a new resource group.
options.note: Deployments never move resources.

explanation: Complete deployment mode makes the resource group match the template exactly, so Resource Manager deletes resources in the group that aren't in the template, like this storage account. Locked resources are the exception. Incremental mode, the default, leaves resources that aren't in the template untouched.

refs.title: Deployment modes

scenario: Before deploying a modified Bicep file to production, you want to preview which resources will be created, changed or deleted without making any changes. What should you run?

options.note: Validate checks syntax and some rules, but doesn't show resource-level changes.
Exports the current state; no comparison.
Compiles Bicep to JSON; no comparison with Azure.

explanation: The what-if operation compares the template with what's currently deployed and lists every resource that would be created, modified, deleted, or left unchanged, without changing anything. Run az deployment group what-if in the CLI or add -WhatIf to New-AzResourceGroupDeployment in PowerShell. Validate only checks syntax and that the deployment would be accepted.

refs.title: Bicep What-If: Preview Changes Before Deployment

scenario: You have an existing ARM JSON template and want to convert it to Bicep for easier maintenance. What should you use?

options.note: Build goes the other way: Bicep to JSON.
The syntax is different.
Moves resources between regions.

explanation: az bicep decompile converts an ARM JSON template into a Bicep file. It's a best-effort conversion, so review the output; some expressions or names may need manual cleanup. az bicep build does the opposite, compiling Bicep into ARM JSON.

refs.title: Decompile a JSON Azure Resource Manager template to Bicep

scenario: A template parameter must receive an admin password from Azure Key Vault at deployment time, without the password appearing in the parameter file. What must the Key Vault allow?

options.text: Access for Azure Resource Manager template deployment
Public network access from all networks on the secret
options.note: Never expose secrets publicly.

options.text: Access for Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption
options.note: That setting is for ADE, not deployments.

options.text: A ReadOnly lock on the vault.
options.note: Locks don't grant access.

explanation: A parameter file can reference a Key Vault secret by vault ID and secret name, so the password never appears in the file. Resource Manager reads the secret during deployment only if the vault has Azure Resource Manager for template deployment enabled and the person deploying has permission on the vault.

refs.title: Key Vault secret with template

scenario: You need to reuse the template that created a resource group's current resources as a starting point for a new environment. What is the quickest way to get it?

options.text: Export template on the resource group
Download the JSON from the Activity log's deployment entries
options.note: Lists operations, not templates.
Advisor doesn't generate templates.
Runs scripts inside VMs.

explanation: Export template on a resource group generates an ARM template (or Bicep) describing the resources it currently contains. It's the quickest starting point for a new environment, but expect to clean it up, for example by turning hard-coded names into parameters and removing properties that can't be exported.

refs.title: Export template in Azure portal

scenario: Which ARM template section declares values that are computed once and reused within the template, such as a combined storage account name?

options.note: Parameters are provided at deployment time.
Outputs return values after deployment.
Declares the resources to deploy.

explanation: The variables section defines values that are computed once from parameters, functions or constants, such as concat('st', uniqueString(resourceGroup().id)). You can then reuse them throughout the template without repeating the expression. Parameters are supplied at deployment time, and outputs return values after deployment.

refs.title: Variables in templates

scenario: You need to sign in to Azure VMs over RDP and SSH from the Azure portal, without public IP addresses on the VMs and without a VPN. What should you deploy?

options.text: Azure Bastion in the virtual network
A public load balancer with inbound NAT rules
options.note: Exposes RDP and SSH to the internet.
Outbound only.
For HTTP(S) apps, not RDP/SSH.

explanation: Azure Bastion is a managed service deployed into your VNet that gives RDP and SSH to VMs over TLS straight from the Azure portal (or a native client), using the VMs' private IPs. The VMs need no public IP, agent or VPN. It's deployed into a dedicated subnet named AzureBastionSubnet.

refs.title: What is Azure Bastion?

scenario: You're deploying Azure Bastion. Which subnet configuration is required?

options.note: Wrong name and too small.
Reserved for VPN and ExpressRoute gateways.

options.text: Any subnet, as long as it has an NSG
options.note: The name and size are mandatory.

explanation: Azure Bastion needs a dedicated subnet named exactly AzureBastionSubnet, sized /26 or larger, with no other resources in it. The Developer SKU is the exception: it's a free shared option that needs neither a dedicated subnet nor a public IP. GatewaySubnet is reserved for VPN and ExpressRoute gateways.

refs.title: About Azure Bastion configuration settings: Azure Bastion subnet

scenario: A VM stopped responding and you can't connect over RDP. You want to see a screenshot of its console to check whether it's stuck at boot. What must be enabled?

options.note: Doesn't give a console view.
Network performance only.
Doesn't help when the OS is stuck.

explanation: Boot diagnostics captures a screenshot of the VM's console and its serial log, so you can see whether it's stuck at a boot screen, an update, or a blue screen. You need it enabled to view the screenshot, and it's also required for the interactive Serial console.

refs.title: Azure boot diagnostics

scenario: You need to reset the local administrator password on a Windows VM that you can't sign in to. What is the simplest built-in method?

options.text: Use 'Reset password' in the portal (VMAccess extension).
Delete the VM and recreate it from the OS disk.
options.note: Far more disruptive.
Diagnostic only.
Doesn't change credentials.

explanation: Reset password in the portal uses the VMAccess extension, running through the VM agent, to reset the local administrator password (or SSH key on Linux). It can also reset the Remote Desktop configuration. You don't need to sign in to the VM or rebuild it.

refs.title: Reset Remote Desktop Services or its Admin Password on a Windows VM

scenario: You need to run a PowerShell script inside a VM to collect diagnostics. The VM has no inbound network access. What should you use?

options.note: Needs network reachability to the VM.
Tests NSG rules; doesn't run scripts.
Interactive and not designed for running scripts.

explanation: Run command executes a PowerShell or shell script inside the VM through the VM agent and the Azure control plane, then returns the output. The VM needs no inbound ports or network path from you. Bastion would still need network access to the VM, and IP flow verify only tests NSG rules.

refs.title: Run scripts in a Windows VM in Azure using action Run Commands

scenario: You redeploy a VM to fix a host-related issue. What happens to data on the VM's temporary disk (D: on Windows)?

options.note: The temporary disk is local to the host.

options.text: It's moved to the OS disk.
options.note: Never happens automatically.

options.text: It's backed up automatically to a storage account.
options.note: No automatic backup.

explanation: Redeploy moves the VM to a new Azure host and restarts it there. The temporary disk (D: on Windows) is local storage on the old host, so everything on it is lost, just as when a VM is deallocated. OS and data disks are managed disks in Azure Storage and are kept.

refs.title: Redeploy Windows virtual machines in Azure

scenario: You create a Windows VM image to deploy many identical VMs. What must you do before capturing a generalized image?

options.note: Not required to capture an image.
Encrypted VMs complicate imaging.
Not required.

explanation: Sysprep with the generalize option removes machine-specific information, such as the computer SID and name, so every VM created from the image is unique. After you capture it, the source VM is marked generalized and can't be started again. On Linux, use waagent -deprovision+user instead.

refs.title: Deprovision or generalize a VM before creating an image

scenario: You need to share VM images with other subscriptions in your tenant and replicate them to several regions with versioning. What should you use?

options.note: No built-in versioning, regional replication or sharing model.
For container images.
Templates describe resources, not disk images.

explanation: Azure Compute Gallery stores image definitions and numbered image versions, and replicates each version to the regions you choose. You share images with other subscriptions through RBAC, direct sharing or community galleries. Storing raw VHDs in a storage account gives you none of that versioning, replication or sharing.

refs.title: Overview of Azure Compute Gallery

scenario: You need to run a batch workload on the cheapest VMs possible. The workload can tolerate interruptions. What should you use, and what can happen?

options.text: Spot VMs; they can be evicted with 30 seconds' notice.
Reserved instances; they may be paused at night.
options.note: Reservations don't pause VMs.

options.text: B-series VMs; they're guaranteed never to be interrupted.
options.note: Burstable VMs are a size family, not a pricing model.

options.text: Dedicated hosts; they're the cheapest option.
options.note: Dedicated hosts cost more.

explanation: Spot VMs run on Azure's spare capacity at a deep discount, which suits interruptible batch work. Azure can evict them with 30 seconds' notice when it needs the capacity back, or when the price rises above your maximum. You choose whether evicted VMs are deallocated or deleted.

refs.title: About Azure Spot Virtual Machines

scenario: You need the highest-performance managed disk for a database's log files, with sub-millisecond latency and IOPS adjustable without downtime. Which disk type fits, and what is one limitation?

options.text: Ultra Disk; it can't be used as an OS disk.
Standard HDD; it doesn't support snapshots.
options.note: Standard HDD is the lowest-performance tier.

options.text: Premium SSD; it can't be resized.
options.note: Premium SSDs can be resized.

options.text: Standard SSD; it can't be attached to VMs.
options.note: Standard SSDs attach to VMs.

explanation: Ultra Disk offers sub-millisecond latency, and you can change its IOPS and throughput without detaching the disk or restarting the VM. That suits database log files well. It can only be used as a data disk, never as an OS disk. Premium SSD v2 has the same data-disk-only limit.

refs.title: Select a disk type for Azure IaaS VMs: Ultra Disks

scenario: You need to decrease the size of a 512 GiB managed data disk to 256 GiB. What is true?

options.text: You can shrink it in the portal after stopping the VM.
options.note: Managed disks can't be shrunk.

options.text: You can't shrink it; create a new disk and copy the data.
Shrinking happens automatically if the disk is mostly empty.
options.note: Disks don't auto-shrink.

options.text: Change the disk type to Standard HDD to shrink it.
options.note: Changing type doesn't change size.

explanation: Azure can expand a managed disk, but it can't shrink one. To end up with a 256 GiB disk, create a new disk of that size, attach it, copy the data across, then swap the disks and delete the old one. Changing the disk type changes performance and price, not size.

refs.title: Expand Virtual Hard Disks Attached to a Windows VM in Azure

scenario: You want to move a running VM and its dependencies from East US to West Europe with minimal manual work. Which service is designed for this?

options.note: Moving a resource group doesn't change the region of its resources.
Connectivity only.
Governs configuration; doesn't move resources.

explanation: Azure Resource Mover moves resources between Azure regions. It works out dependencies such as the VNet, NSGs and public IPs, moves them together, and uses Site Recovery replication to copy VMs with minimal downtime. Moving a resource group or subscription never changes a resource's region.

refs.title: What is Azure Resource Mover?
Move Azure VMs across regions with Azure Resource Mover

scenario: Your web app on App Service needs a staging environment where you can test new releases and then swap into production with no downtime. Which App Service plan tier is the minimum?

options.note: No deployment slots.
No deployment slots.
No deployment slots.

explanation: Deployment slots need the Standard tier or higher: Standard gives 5 slots and Premium gives 20. A swap warms up the staging slot first and then switches routing between the slots, so production has no downtime. If the new release misbehaves, swapping back restores the previous version.

refs.title: Set Up Staging Environments

scenario: After a slot swap, production started using the staging database connection string. The connection string should always stay with its slot. What should you configure?

options.text: Mark it as a deployment slot setting.
Store it in the web.config only.
options.note: Config files move with the deployed code.

options.text: Use a different App Service plan for staging.
options.note: Doesn't control what moves during a swap.
Doesn't stop settings from swapping.

explanation: By default, app settings and connection strings move with the app when you swap slots. Selecting Deployment slot setting makes one "sticky", so it stays with its slot and production keeps the production database connection string after every swap.

refs.title: Set Up Staging Environments: Which settings are swapped

scenario: You need an App Service web app to scale out automatically based on CPU load. What is the minimum App Service plan tier for autoscale?

options.note: No scale-out.
Basic supports manual scale-out only (up to 3 instances).
Runs on shared infrastructure without scaling.

explanation: Rule-based autoscale, such as adding instances when CPU is high, needs the Standard tier or higher; Basic only supports manual scaling. Premium v2 and v3 also offer automatic scaling, which scales on HTTP traffic without writing rules.

refs.title: Scale Up Features and Capacities
Get started with autoscale in Azure

scenario: Three web apps share one App Service plan. You scale the plan up from S1 to P1v3. What is affected?

options.text: Only the first app in the plan.
options.note: The plan's resources are shared by all apps.

options.text: All three apps, since they run on the plan's instances.
None of them until each app is restarted manually.
options.note: The change applies automatically.
All apps in the plan are affected.

explanation: An App Service plan is the set of VM instances its apps run on, and every app in the plan runs on all of those instances. Scaling the plan up (to P1v3) or out (more instances) therefore affects all three apps at once. If one app needs to scale on its own, move it to its own plan.

refs.title: Azure App Service Plans

scenario: You need to bind a custom domain with a TLS/SSL certificate to an App Service web app. What is the minimum pricing tier?

options.note: Doesn't support custom domains.
Works, but Basic is enough.
Works, but Basic is enough.

explanation: Custom domains with TLS/SSL bindings need the Basic tier or higher; the Free and Shared tiers can't bind certificates. You verify ownership of the domain with a CNAME (or A) record plus a TXT verification record, then add a certificate, such as a free App Service managed certificate.

refs.title: Set Up an Existing Custom Domain Name for Your App
Secure Your Domain with TLS/SSL

scenario: You want container images in Azure Container Registry to be replicated to registries in three regions, so nearby deployments pull them quickly. Which ACR tier is required?

options.note: No geo-replication.
No geo-replication.

options.text: Any tier, with a lifecycle rule
options.note: Lifecycle rules don't replicate registries.

explanation: Geo-replication is a Premium-tier feature of Azure Container Registry. You push an image once and ACR replicates it to every configured region, so deployments in each region pull from a nearby replica under one registry name. Private endpoints are also Premium-only.

refs.title: Geo-replication in Azure Container Registry
Azure Container Registry SKU Features and Limits

scenario: An ACI deployment needs a web container plus a logging sidecar that share the same IP address, lifecycle and local network. How should you deploy them?

options.text: As two containers in one container group.
As two separate container groups with VNet peering.
options.note: Separate groups don't share an IP or lifecycle.
Not ACI.
Not containers.

explanation: A container group is a set of containers scheduled together on the same host. They share one IP address and port namespace, local network (so the sidecar reaches the app on localhost), storage volumes and lifecycle. That's the sidecar pattern in ACI. Multi-container groups are currently supported for Linux containers.

refs.title: Introduction to container groups

scenario: Data written by an Azure Container Instances container must survive restarts and be shared with other services. What should you mount?

options.text: An Azure file share as a volume

options.note: Lost when the container restarts.
Shared within the group, but not persistent beyond its lifetime.
Clones a repo at startup; it isn't persistent storage.

explanation: A container's own file system is lost when it restarts. Mounting an Azure file share as a volume gives the container persistent storage that survives restarts and that other services or containers can also reach. You supply the storage account name, share name and key in the volume definition.

refs.title: Mount Azure Files volume to container group

scenario: A containerized API on Azure Container Apps gets no traffic overnight. You want to pay nothing for compute when idle and scale up automatically on HTTP requests. What should you configure?

options.text: Min replicas 0 with an HTTP scale rule
Min replicas 3 with a CPU scale rule
options.note: Keeps replicas running all night.
Plans are billed while they exist.
Breaks the app and doesn't affect scaling costs.

explanation: Azure Container Apps scales with KEDA-based rules such as HTTP concurrency, queue length or custom metrics. With minimum replicas set to 0, the app scales to zero when idle, so you pay nothing for compute overnight, and the HTTP scale rule starts replicas again when requests arrive.

refs.title: Scaling in Azure Container Apps

scenario: Pods in an AKS cluster are stuck in Pending because the nodes are out of CPU. You want the cluster to add nodes automatically when pods can't be scheduled. What should you enable?

options.text: The cluster autoscaler on the node pool

options.note: HPA adds pods, which then stay Pending with no capacity.

options.text: A VM Scale Set autoscale rule outside AKS
options.note: AKS manages its node pools; use the cluster autoscaler.
Unrelated to capacity.

explanation: The cluster autoscaler watches for pods stuck in Pending because no node has room, adds nodes to the node pool up to its maximum count, and removes underused nodes later. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler only changes the number of pod replicas, which doesn't help when the nodes are full.

refs.title: Use the Cluster Autoscaler in Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)

scenario: You need to add GPU-enabled nodes to an existing AKS cluster for a machine learning workload, without changing the existing nodes. What should you do?

options.text: Add a new user node pool with a GPU VM size.
Resize all nodes in the system node pool to GPU sizes.
options.note: Changes existing nodes and wastes GPU capacity.

options.text: Create a new cluster for every model.
options.note: Unnecessary overhead.
Adds more nodes of the same size.

explanation: Node pools let one AKS cluster run nodes of different VM sizes. Adding a new user node pool with a GPU VM size leaves the existing nodes untouched. Taint the GPU pool and give the ML pods a matching toleration (or a node selector) so only GPU workloads land there.

refs.title: Create Node Pools in Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
Use GPUs on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)

scenario: A VM Scale Set must mix Spot and regular VMs, and allow different VM sizes in the same set. Which orchestration mode should you use?

options.note: Uniform uses identical instances from one model.
Not a scale set orchestration mode.
Controls placement, not orchestration.

explanation: Flexible orchestration manages standard Azure VMs in the scale set. It supports mixing Spot and regular (on-demand) instances, using more than one VM size, and spreading VMs across zones or fault domains. Uniform mode uses identical instances of a single size, and Microsoft recommends Flexible for new scale sets.

refs.title: Orchestration modes for Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Azure

scenario: You need to run 10 VMs that can tolerate one physical rack failing, in a region without availability zones. What should you use?

options.text: A single large VM with Premium SSD disks
options.note: One VM can't survive a rack failure.
Packs VMs close together.
Locks don't affect physical placement.

explanation: An availability set spreads VMs across fault domains, which are separate racks with their own power and network switch, and across update domains for planned maintenance. If one rack fails, only the VMs in that fault domain go down. With two or more VMs in an availability set, the SLA is 99.95%.

refs.title: Availability sets overview

scenario: You create a subnet with the prefix 10.0.1.0/24. How many IP addresses can you assign to VMs and other resources in it?

options.note: Azure reserves some addresses in every subnet.
Azure reserves more than just the network and broadcast addresses.
Azure reserves exactly 5 addresses.

explanation: Azure reserves 5 addresses in every subnet: the network address (.0), the default gateway (.1), two addresses for Azure DNS (.2 and .3), and the broadcast address (.255). A /24 has 256 addresses, so 256 − 5 = 251 can be assigned to VMs and other resources.

refs.title: Azure Virtual Network FAQ: Are there any restrictions on using IP addresses within these subnets?

scenario: What is the smallest subnet size Azure supports for a virtual network subnet?

options.note: Too small; Azure needs 5 reserved addresses.
Valid, but not the smallest.
A single address.

explanation: The smallest subnet Azure supports is /29, which has 8 addresses, only 3 of them usable after Azure reserves 5. Many services need more: Azure Bastion and Azure Firewall need /26, and Microsoft recommends /27 or larger for gateway subnets.

refs.title: Azure Virtual Network FAQ: How small and how large can virtual networks and subnets be?

scenario: A VNet uses 10.0.0.0/16. You need to peer it with another VNet that uses 10.0.128.0/17. What will happen?

options.note: The ranges overlap.

options.text: Peering fails because the address spaces overlap.
Peering works, but only for UDP traffic.
options.note: No such restriction exists.

options.text: Peering works only if both VNets are in the same region.
options.note: The overlap blocks peering in any region.

explanation: 10.0.128.0/17 covers 10.0.128.0 to 10.0.255.255, which is entirely inside 10.0.0.0/16 (10.0.0.0 to 10.0.255.255). Peered VNets can't have overlapping address spaces, because routing between them would be ambiguous, so the peering fails. Plan non-overlapping ranges before connecting networks.

refs.title: Create, Change, or Delete Azure Virtual Network Peering: Requirements and constraints

scenario: VNet A is peered with VNet B, and VNet B is peered with VNet C. VMs in A can't reach VMs in C. Why?

options.text: Peering supports only two VNets per subscription.
options.note: There's no such limit.
Not required.

options.text: The VNets must be in different regions.
options.note: Region doesn't matter.

explanation: VNet peering isn't transitive: each peering connects only the two VNets in that pair, so A peered with B and B peered with C doesn't connect A to C. Either peer A and C directly, route through a hub using an NVA or Azure Firewall with user-defined routes, or use Azure Virtual WAN.

refs.title: Azure Virtual Network Peering
Hub-spoke network topology in Azure

scenario: Spoke VNets peered with a hub VNet must use the hub's VPN gateway to reach on-premises networks. Which peering settings are required?

options.text: Hub: Allow gateway transit; spokes: Use remote gateways
Hub and spokes: Use remote gateways
options.note: Only the spoke uses the remote gateway; the hub allows transit.

options.text: Deploy a VPN gateway in every spoke.
options.note: Works, but defeats the purpose of a shared hub gateway.

options.text: Hub and spokes: Allow forwarded traffic only
options.note: Not enough on its own to use the gateway.

explanation: Gateway transit lets peered VNets share one VPN or ExpressRoute gateway. Turn on Allow gateway transit on the hub side of the peering and Use remote gateways on each spoke side. A spoke that uses the hub's gateway can't have a gateway of its own.

refs.title: Configure VPN gateway transit for virtual network peering

scenario: Two NSGs apply to a VM: one on its subnet and one on its NIC. The subnet NSG allows inbound TCP 443, and the NIC NSG has only the default rules. Can clients reach the VM on port 443 from the internet?

options.text: Yes, because the subnet NSG allows it.
options.note: Inbound traffic must be allowed by both NSGs.

options.text: No, the NIC NSG's default DenyAllInBound blocks it.
Yes, NIC NSGs are ignored when a subnet NSG exists.
options.note: Both are evaluated.

options.text: Only if accelerated networking is enabled.
options.note: Unrelated.

explanation: For inbound traffic, Azure checks the subnet NSG first and then the NIC NSG, and the traffic must be allowed by both. The subnet NSG allows 443, but the NIC NSG only has default rules, so its DenyAllInBound (priority 65500) blocks the connection. Effective security rules on the NIC shows the combined result.

refs.title: How Network Security Groups Filter Network Traffic in Azure

scenario: Which default inbound NSG rule allows health probes from Azure Load Balancer to reach backend VMs?

options.note: Covers traffic inside the virtual network.
Denies traffic.
There's no such default rule.

explanation: Every NSG has three default inbound rules: AllowVnetInBound (65000), AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound (65001) and DenyAllInBound (65500). AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound lets health probes from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag (168.63.129.16) reach backend VMs. You can override default rules with custom rules that have lower priority numbers, but you can't delete them.

refs.title: Azure network security groups overview: Default security rules

scenario: You need an NSG rule that allows outbound traffic from VMs to Azure Storage in any region, without maintaining IP lists. What should you use as the destination?

options.note: ASGs group your own VM NICs, not Azure services.
Far broader than needed.
Allows everything.

explanation: A service tag represents the IP prefixes of an Azure service, and Microsoft keeps them up to date. Using the Storage tag as the destination in an outbound rule allows traffic to Azure Storage in every region, with no IP lists for you to maintain. Regional tags such as Storage.EastUS narrow it to one region.

refs.title: Azure service tags overview

scenario: A VM can't reach the internet, and you suspect a user-defined route is sending traffic somewhere unexpected. Which tool shows the next hop for traffic from the VM to a specific IP address?

options.note: Checks NSG rules, not routing.
Not a network diagnostic tool.
Don't show routing decisions.

explanation: Network Watcher's Next hop tool shows where traffic from a VM to a given destination IP will go: the next hop type (Internet, VirtualAppliance, VirtualNetworkGateway, None and so on), its IP address, and the route table that chose it. That quickly exposes a misdirected user-defined route. The NIC's Effective routes shows the full route list.

refs.title: Next Hop Overview

scenario: Traffic from a subnet to 10.50.0.0/16 must be dropped entirely. What should you add to the subnet's route table?

options.text: A route to 10.50.0.0/16 with next hop type None
A route to 10.50.0.0/16 with next hop type Internet
options.note: Sends the traffic to the internet.

options.text: A route with next hop type Virtual network
options.note: Keeps the traffic in the VNet.
Unrelated to routing.

explanation: A user-defined route with next hop type None drops all traffic sent to that prefix, so a route for 10.50.0.0/16 with next hop None blocks it entirely. The other next hop types (Virtual appliance, Virtual network gateway, Virtual network, Internet) all forward the traffic somewhere.

refs.title: Azure virtual network traffic routing

scenario: Which statement about Standard SKU public IP addresses is correct?

options.text: They block inbound traffic unless an NSG allows it.

options.note: Standard public IPs are always static.
They can be zonal or zone-redundant.

options.text: They are open to all inbound traffic by default.
options.note: That was Basic SKU behavior; Basic is retired.

explanation: Standard SKU public IPs are always static and secure by default: inbound traffic is blocked until an NSG on the NIC or subnet allows it. They also support zone-redundant and zonal deployment. Basic SKU public IPs, which were open by default, were retired on September 30, 2025.

refs.title: Public IP addresses in Azure: SKU

scenario: Your company bought the domain contoso.com from a third-party registrar. You create a public Azure DNS zone for contoso.com. What else must you do so Azure DNS answers queries for the domain?

options.text: Update the NS records at the registrar
Create a private DNS zone with the same name.
options.note: Private zones aren't resolvable from the internet.

options.text: Create an @ A record and a www CNAME in the zone
options.note: Records won't be found until the domain is delegated.

options.text: Link the zone to the virtual network hosting the web servers
options.note: Only private zones are linked to VNets.

explanation: Azure DNS hosts the zone, but the internet only sends queries for contoso.com to Azure once the domain is delegated. Delegate it by replacing the name server (NS) records at your registrar with the four Azure DNS name servers listed on the zone. Azure DNS isn't a registrar, so this step happens at the third-party registrar.

refs.title: Tutorial: Host your domain in Azure DNS

scenario: You want www.contoso.com to point to the web app contoso-web.azurewebsites.net. Which DNS record type should you create?

options.note: An A record maps to an IP address.
For mail routing.
Used for verification, not aliasing.

explanation: A CNAME record maps one name to another, so www.contoso.com can point to contoso-web.azurewebsites.net and keep working if the app's IP changes. CNAMEs can't be used at the zone apex (contoso.com itself). There, an Azure DNS alias record or an A record does the job.

refs.title: DNS Zones and Records Overview: DNS records
Set Up an Existing Custom Domain Name for Your App

scenario: A private DNS zone corp.internal is linked to two VNets. VMs in VNet1 should get DNS records created automatically when they're deployed; VNet2 only needs to resolve names. How should the links be configured?

options.text: Enable auto-registration on the VNet1 link only.
Enable auto-registration on the VNet2 link only.
options.note: Works, but VNet2 only needs resolution.

options.text: Disable both links and use hosts files.
options.note: Defeats the purpose of private DNS.

options.text: Create a public zone for VNet2.
options.note: Public zones aren't for internal names.

explanation: Each virtual network link to a private DNS zone is either a registration link (auto-registration on) or a resolution-only link. Turn auto-registration on for the VNet1 link only, so VNet1's VMs get records automatically, while VNet2 can still resolve the names. A VNet can have auto-registration on for only one private DNS zone.

refs.title: What is a virtual network link subresource of Azure DNS private zones

scenario: VMs behind a public Standard Load Balancer need RDP access on port 3389, but only one VM should be reachable on frontend port 50001. What should you configure?

options.text: A load-balancing rule from port 50001 to 3389
options.note: Spreads RDP across all backends.
Controls outbound SNAT only.
Probes don't forward traffic.

explanation: An inbound NAT rule forwards one frontend port on the load balancer (50001) to a specific backend VM and port (3389), so you can reach that one VM directly. A load-balancing rule would spread port 50001 across every backend VM instead. Azure Bastion is usually the more secure way to give RDP access.

refs.title: Inbound NAT rules

scenario: Two network virtual appliances behind an internal Standard Load Balancer must receive all TCP and UDP traffic on all ports, for high availability. What should you use?

options.text: One load-balancing rule per port (65,535 rules)
options.note: Impractical and exceeds limits.
Basic is retired and doesn't support HA ports.
Floating IP alone doesn't cover all ports.

explanation: An HA ports rule on an internal Standard Load Balancer (protocol All, port 0) load-balances every TCP and UDP flow on every port with a single rule. That's the standard design for active-active network virtual appliances. The alternative of one rule per port isn't practical, and Basic load balancers don't support HA ports.

refs.title: High availability ports overview in Azure

scenario: A load balancer health probe fails for every backend VM, so no traffic is forwarded. The app on the VMs is running. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether the probe port is blocked
Whether each backend VM has its own public IP address
options.note: Backend VMs don't need public IPs.

options.text: Whether the storage account is GRS.
options.note: Unrelated.

options.text: Whether the VMs are in the same resource group.
options.note: Doesn't matter.

explanation: Health probes come from Azure's infrastructure IP 168.63.129.16 (the AzureLoadBalancer service tag). If an NSG or the guest OS firewall blocks the probe port, or an HTTP probe path doesn't return 200, every backend is marked unhealthy and no traffic is forwarded, even though the app is running.

refs.title: Azure Load Balancer health probes

scenario: One Application Gateway must send requests for /images/* to one backend pool and /video/* to another. What should you configure?

options.text: A path-based routing rule with a URL path map

options.note: Layer 4 load balancers can't route by URL path.
DNS-level only; can't see URL paths.
Keeps a user on one backend; no path routing.

explanation: Application Gateway is a layer 7 (HTTP) load balancer. A path-based routing rule uses a URL path map to send /images/* to one backend pool and /video/* to another. Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4 and can't see URL paths.

refs.title: Azure Application Gateway URL-based content routing overview

scenario: A global web app runs in three regions. You need a single entry point that routes users to the closest healthy backend, caches static content at the edge, and includes WAF. What should you use?

options.note: Regional and layer 4.
Regional, not global.
Outbound only.

explanation: Azure Front Door is a global layer 7 entry point. Users connect to the nearest Microsoft edge location, traffic goes to the closest healthy backend based on latency and health probes, and Front Door can cache static content at the edge and apply WAF rules. Traffic Manager is DNS-only, with no caching or WAF.

refs.title: Azure Front Door Overview

scenario: You want DNS-based routing that sends all users to the primary region and fails over to a secondary region only if the primary is unhealthy, for a non-HTTP service. What should you use?

options.text: Traffic Manager with the Priority routing method

options.note: Splits traffic by weight; not primary/secondary.
Regional and HTTP only.
Front Door is designed for HTTP(S) traffic.

explanation: Traffic Manager routes at the DNS level, so it works for any protocol, not just HTTP. With the Priority routing method, every user is sent to the primary endpoint, and Traffic Manager only answers with the secondary when health checks show the primary is down. Application Gateway and Front Door are for HTTP(S).

refs.title: Traffic Manager Routing Methods: Priority traffic-routing method

scenario: Remote employees on laptops need to connect securely to an Azure VNet from home using their Microsoft Entra credentials. What should you configure?

options.text: A point-to-site VPN with Entra ID authentication
A site-to-site VPN to each employee's home router
options.note: Connects whole networks through a VPN device, not individual laptops.
Connects VNets, not remote clients.
A dedicated circuit for sites, not individual users.

explanation: A point-to-site VPN connects individual devices to the VNet from anywhere. With Microsoft Entra ID authentication (OpenVPN protocol, Azure VPN Client), employees sign in with their Entra credentials, and Conditional Access and MFA can apply. Site-to-site connects whole networks, not individual laptops.

refs.title: Configure P2S VPN gateway for Microsoft Entra ID authentication: Microsoft-registered client
About Azure Point-to-Site VPN connections

scenario: You need a site-to-site VPN plus point-to-site connections and multiple site-to-site tunnels. Which VPN type must the virtual network gateway use?

options.note: Supports only one S2S tunnel and no P2S.

options.text: Either; they support the same features
options.note: Policy-based has major limitations.
A different gateway type.

explanation: Route-based VPN gateways support multiple site-to-site tunnels, point-to-site, VNet-to-VNet, BGP and coexistence with ExpressRoute. Policy-based gateways support only a single site-to-site tunnel with static policies, and no point-to-site. You can't change the VPN type after the gateway is created.

refs.title: Azure VPN Gateway configuration settings: VPN types

scenario: When you create a VPN gateway, which subnet must exist in the VNet?

options.note: The name must be GatewaySubnet.
Reserved for Azure Firewall.
Gateways require GatewaySubnet.

explanation: VPN and ExpressRoute gateways are deployed into a subnet that must be named exactly GatewaySubnet. Microsoft recommends /27 or larger to leave room for future configurations. Don't deploy anything else into it, and don't associate an NSG with it.

refs.title: Azure VPN Gateway configuration settings: Gateway subnet

scenario: You need a private, dedicated connection from your datacenter to Azure that doesn't go over the public internet, with predictable latency and up to 10 Gbps. What should you use?

options.note: Runs encrypted over the public internet.
For individual clients over the internet.
Connects Azure VNets only.

explanation: ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated connection from your datacenter to Microsoft through a connectivity provider. It doesn't cross the public internet and gives predictable latency, with bandwidths up to 10 Gbps (100 Gbps with ExpressRoute Direct). Private peering reaches your VNets. A site-to-site VPN runs over the internet.

refs.title: Azure ExpressRoute Overview: Connect over a private connection

scenario: You deploy Azure Firewall to filter traffic for spoke VNets. Which subnet requirement applies?

options.note: Wrong name and too small.
Reserved for gateways.
Reserved for Bastion.

explanation: Azure Firewall needs a dedicated subnet named exactly AzureFirewallSubnet, sized /26 or larger. The spoke subnets then get a user-defined route for 0.0.0.0/0 with the firewall's private IP as the next hop, so their traffic passes through it.

refs.title: Deploy & configure Azure Firewall using the Azure portal

scenario: VMs must reach a storage account through the Azure backbone, and the storage firewall must allow only that subnet. You don't need a private IP for the storage account. What is the simplest option?

options.text: A service endpoint plus a storage firewall rule
Create a private endpoint and private DNS zone.
options.note: Also works, but adds a private IP and DNS setup you said you don't need.
Unnecessary.

options.text: Set public network access to 'Enabled from all networks'.
options.note: Allows everyone.

explanation: A service endpoint extends the subnet's identity to Azure Storage over the Azure backbone, so the storage firewall can allow just that subnet. The account keeps its public IP. Service endpoints are free and quick to set up. A private endpoint is the better choice only when you need a private IP or access from on-premises.

refs.title: Azure virtual network service endpoints
Firewall rules and network access for Azure Blob, Data Lake, Queue, and Table Storage

scenario: After creating a private endpoint for a storage account, VMs still connect to its public IP address. What is the most likely missing piece?

options.text: The privatelink private DNS zone and VNet link
An outbound NSG rule allowing 443 to the endpoint
options.note: Outbound 443 is allowed by default.

options.text: A public IP on the private endpoint.
options.note: Private endpoints don't use public IPs.
Unrelated.

explanation: A private endpoint only works if clients resolve the storage account's name to the endpoint's private IP. That record lives in the privatelink.blob.core.windows.net private DNS zone, which must be linked to the VNet. Without it, the name still resolves to the public IP. On-premises clients need conditional forwarding, for example through Azure DNS Private Resolver.

refs.title: Azure Private Endpoint private DNS zone values

scenario: On-premises DNS servers must resolve names in Azure private DNS zones, and Azure VMs must resolve on-premises names, without running DNS server VMs. What should you deploy?

options.note: Exposes internal names publicly.

options.text: Hosts files on every Azure VM and on-premises server
options.note: Unmanageable.
Global traffic routing, not DNS forwarding.

explanation: Azure DNS Private Resolver gives you managed DNS endpoints in your VNet, with no VMs to run. On-premises DNS servers forward queries for Azure private zones to its inbound endpoint. Its outbound endpoint, with a forwarding ruleset, sends Azure VMs' queries for on-premises domains to your DNS servers.

refs.title: Azure DNS Private Resolver Overview

scenario: A VM's NIC needs to forward traffic it receives for other destinations, because it runs firewall software. What must be enabled in Azure?

options.note: Improves performance; doesn't allow forwarding.
Not required for forwarding.
A load balancer setting.

explanation: By default Azure drops any packet whose destination isn't the IP address of the NIC that received it. Enabling IP forwarding on the NIC, and turning on routing inside the operating system, lets the VM pass traffic along to other destinations, which is how an NVA or firewall VM works.

refs.title: Create, Change, or Delete Azure Network Interfaces: Enable or disable IP forwarding

scenario: Which statement about NSG rule priority numbers for custom rules is correct?

options.text: Custom rules can use priorities 100–4096, and lower numbers are processed first.
Custom rules can use 1–65500, and higher numbers are processed first.
options.note: Wrong range and order.

options.text: All rules are evaluated, and Deny always wins.
options.note: Processing stops at the first match.

options.text: Priority only matters for outbound rules.
options.note: It applies to both directions.

explanation: Custom NSG rules use priorities from 100 to 4096. Azure processes them from the lowest number to the highest and stops at the first match, so a lower number always takes precedence. Two rules in the same direction can't share a priority, and the default rules sit at 65000 and above.

refs.title: Azure network security groups overview: Security rules

scenario: Users report intermittent failures connecting from a VM to an external API. You want to test TCP connectivity to api.contoso.com:443 from the VM and see where on the path it fails. Which Network Watcher tool is best for a one-time check?

options.note: Shows routing only.
Shows resource relationships only.
Shows NSG rules but doesn't test a connection.

explanation: Connection troubleshoot runs a one-time check from a VM to a destination host and port, such as api.contoso.com:443. It reports whether the connection succeeds, its latency and hops, and problems it finds, such as an NSG rule blocking traffic, a bad route or a DNS failure. Connection monitor runs the same kind of test continuously.

refs.title: Connection Troubleshoot Overview

scenario: Auditors need a record of who deleted resources in a subscription over the last 2 years. By default, how long are Activity log events kept, and what should you do?

options.text: 90 days; export it with a diagnostic setting

options.note: The platform keeps Activity log events for only 90 days.

options.text: 30 days; enable Azure Backup for the subscription
options.note: Backup doesn't protect logs, and the default is 90 days.
Events older than 90 days are removed.

explanation: The Activity log records control-plane operations, such as who deleted which resource and when, and keeps them for 90 days. To keep two years, create a diagnostic setting on the subscription that sends Activity log events to a Log Analytics workspace (with the retention you need), a storage account, or Event Hubs.

refs.title: Activity Log in Azure Monitor
Diagnostic Settings in Azure Monitor

scenario: You need platform metrics for a VM going back more than 3 months for capacity planning. By default, how long does Azure Monitor keep platform metrics?

options.note: Longer than that.
Shorter than that.
Much longer than that.

explanation: Azure Monitor keeps platform metrics for 93 days. For a longer history, send the metrics to a Log Analytics workspace with a diagnostic setting (or a data collection rule for guest OS metrics) and set the workspace retention you need.

refs.title: Metrics in Azure Monitor: Retention of metrics

scenario: A Log Analytics workspace keeps data for the default 30 days. Security wants query access to the last year of data. What should you change?

options.text: Create a second workspace and send data to both
options.note: Doesn't extend retention.
Covers only Activity log data.

options.text: Change the pricing tier to Free.
options.note: The Free tier has shorter retention and a daily cap.

explanation: Each Log Analytics workspace, or individual table, has an interactive (analytics) retention period that defaults to 30 days and can be raised to up to 2 years. Set it to 365 days so security can query a full year. Long-term retention can keep data up to 12 years more cheaply, but you need search jobs or a restore to query it.

refs.title: Manage Data Retention in a Log Analytics Workspace

scenario: You need logs from an Azure SQL database and a Key Vault sent to a Log Analytics workspace. What do you configure on each resource?

options.text: The Azure Monitor Agent, installed through an extension
options.note: The agent runs on VMs, not on PaaS resources.
Defines alert notifications, not log collection.
Unrelated to logging.

explanation: Resource logs, such as SQL database audit and query logs or Key Vault access logs, aren't collected by default. A diagnostic setting on each resource chooses which log categories and metrics to send, and where to send them: Log Analytics, a storage account, Event Hubs or a partner solution. Azure Policy can deploy these settings at scale.

refs.title: Diagnostic Settings in Azure Monitor

scenario: You want an email whenever anyone deletes a virtual machine in the production subscription. Which alert type should you create?

options.text: A metric alert on VM Availability dropping to 0
options.note: Metrics don't record deletions.

options.text: A log search alert on the Perf table
options.note: Perf holds performance counters, not management operations.
Tracks spending.

explanation: Deleting a VM is a control-plane operation recorded in the Activity log, so an Activity log alert on the Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete operation, scoped to the production subscription, fires whenever it happens. Attach an action group that sends the email. Metric alerts can't tell you who deleted something.

refs.title: Types of Azure Monitor alerts: Activity log alerts

scenario: You want to be notified when Azure has a service issue or planned maintenance affecting the regions and services your subscription uses. What should you configure?

options.text: A metric alert on every resource
options.note: Doesn't capture platform incidents.
Not real-time incident notifications.
Routes logs; doesn't send notifications on its own.

explanation: Service Health tracks Azure-wide incidents, planned maintenance, and health and security advisories. A Service Health alert, a type of Activity log alert, notifies you through an action group when an event affects the services and regions you select. It's about Azure's health, not your own resources' metrics.

refs.title: Create Service Health alerts for Azure service notifications

scenario: A single VM became unavailable, and you want to know whether an Azure platform problem caused it, along with its health history. Where should you look first?

options.note: Recommendations, not availability history.
Billing data.
Identity events.

explanation: Resource Health shows the current and past health of one specific resource, such as this VM. It says whether a problem was caused by an Azure platform event or by a user action, and recommends next steps. Service Health covers wider incidents across a service or region.

refs.title: Azure Resource Health overview

scenario: Nightly patching causes many CPU alerts between 01:00 and 03:00 on Sundays. Alerts should still fire and be recorded, but no notifications should be sent during that window. What should you configure?

options.text: An alert processing rule with a schedule
Delete the alert rules and recreate them on Monday
options.note: Error-prone, and alerts wouldn't be recorded.
Hides real problems all week.

options.text: Disable the Azure Monitor Agent during patching
options.note: Stops data collection.

explanation: An alert processing rule can suppress notifications for fired alerts during a schedule, such as Sundays from 01:00 to 03:00, while the alerts themselves still fire and are recorded. It can be scoped to specific resources or alert rules, and can also add action groups instead of suppressing them.

refs.title: Alert processing rules for Azure Monitor alerts

scenario: You need an alert when a VM hasn't sent a heartbeat to Log Analytics for 10 minutes. Which alert type and table should you use?

options.text: A log search alert querying the Heartbeat table
An Activity log alert on VM stop
options.note: Misses OS hangs and agent failures where nothing is stopped.
Covers platform issues only.
Tracks spending.

explanation: Connected agents write a record to the Heartbeat table about once a minute. A log search alert with a query such as Heartbeat | summarize max(TimeGenerated) by Computer | where max_TimeGenerated < ago(10m) finds machines that have gone quiet. Activity log alerts only see control-plane operations.

refs.title: Monitor virtual machines with Azure Monitor: Alerts

scenario: Which KQL query returns the latest heartbeat time for each computer?

options.text: SELECT Computer, MAX(TimeGenerated) FROM Heartbeat GROUP BY Computer
options.note: That's SQL, not KQL.
Not valid logic.
Returns one row overall, not one per computer.

explanation: summarize aggregates rows, and by sets the groups, so summarize LastHeartbeat = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer returns one row per computer with its most recent heartbeat time. KQL isn't SQL, so SELECT and GROUP BY don't work. To get the whole latest row instead of one column, use arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by Computer.

extend adds columns; take limits rows.
A self-join isn't needed.

explanation: bin(TimeGenerated, 5m) rounds each timestamp down into a 5-minute bucket, and summarize avg(CounterValue) by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m), Computer averages CPU within each bucket for each computer. Add | render timechart to draw one line per computer.
