scenario: Which table in a Log Analytics workspace holds Activity log records sent through a diagnostic setting?

options.note: Agent heartbeats.
Performance counters.
Windows event logs from agents.

explanation: Activity log events sent to a Log Analytics workspace through a diagnostic setting land in the AzureActivity table. Heartbeat holds agent heartbeats, Perf holds performance counters, and Event holds Windows event logs collected from inside VMs.

refs.title: Activity Log in Azure Monitor: Export activity log
Azure Monitor Logs reference - AzureActivity

scenario: You want a dependency map that shows the processes and connections between VMs, plus performance charts. What should you enable?

options.text: VM insights with the Map feature

options.note: Shows console output only.
Recommendations only.
Shows Azure resources, not processes and connections inside VMs.

explanation: VM insights shows performance charts from the Azure Monitor Agent. With the Dependency agent installed as well, its Map feature discovers processes running on each VM and the network connections between VMs and external endpoints. Network Watcher topology shows network resources, not processes.

refs.title: Monitor virtual machines in Azure
View app dependencies with VM insights

scenario: You need an interactive report that combines metrics, log queries and text for your operations team, and that they can parameterize by subscription. What should you create?

options.note: Sends notifications.
Defines data collection.
Routes logs.

explanation: Azure Monitor workbooks combine text, KQL log queries, metrics and parameters (such as a subscription drop-down) in one interactive report that you can save and share with the team. Dashboards and Azure Managed Grafana are alternatives for at-a-glance views. Action groups, data collection rules and diagnostic settings don't create reports.

refs.title: Azure Workbooks overview

scenario: NSG flow logs are being retired. Which feature should you use to log IP traffic flowing through a virtual network?

options.note: Control-plane operations only.
VM console output.
Application telemetry.

explanation: Virtual network flow logs record IP traffic at the virtual network level, which covers more scenarios than NSG flow logs, including traffic with no NSG involved. New NSG flow logs can no longer be created, and existing ones retire in 2027. Traffic analytics can visualize VNet flow log data.

refs.title: Virtual Network Flow Logs

scenario: You want to restore a single deleted file from last week's backup of an Azure VM without restoring the whole VM. What should you use?

options.text: Restore the full VM over the existing one
options.note: Overwrites current data.
No access to backups.
Replication for disaster recovery, not item-level restore.

explanation: File Recovery generates a script that mounts the disks from the chosen recovery point as local drives on a machine (over iSCSI). You browse them, copy back only the files you need, and then unmount. There's no need to restore or replace the whole VM.

refs.title: Recover files and folders from Azure VM backup

scenario: You need to back up Azure Blob storage, Azure Disks and Azure Database for PostgreSQL servers. Which vault type supports these workloads?

options.note: Recovery Services vaults handle VMs, SQL in VMs, Azure Files and MARS, not these.
Stores secrets and keys.
Not a backup vault.

explanation: Azure Backup has two vault types. Backup vaults handle newer workloads such as Azure Blob storage, Azure Disks, Azure Database for PostgreSQL and AKS. Recovery Services vaults handle Azure VMs, SQL and SAP HANA running in VMs, Azure Files and on-premises backups.

refs.title: Overview of the Backup vaults

scenario: You need to back up specific folders from an on-premises Windows file server directly to Azure, without System Center or a backup server. What should you install?

options.text: The Azure Monitor Agent, installed through an extension
options.note: Collects telemetry.
Syncs files; it isn't a backup with retention points.
Maps dependencies.

explanation: The Microsoft Azure Recovery Services (MARS) agent installs directly on a Windows machine and backs up files, folders and system state to a Recovery Services vault on a schedule. You don't need System Center DPM or MABS. Azure File Sync syncs files rather than backing them up.

refs.title: About the MARS Agent

scenario: A database VM needs backups every 4 hours. The standard VM backup policy allows only one backup per day. What should you use?

options.text: An Enhanced backup policy with an hourly schedule
Five standard policies on the same VM
options.note: A VM can have only one backup policy.
Applies to blobs.
Affects backup storage redundancy, not frequency.

explanation: Standard VM backup policies take one backup a day. An Enhanced policy supports multiple backups per day, here every 4 hours, plus longer instant-restore retention and Trusted Launch VMs. Several standard policies can't be applied to the same VM.

refs.title: Back Up Azure VMs with the Enhanced Policy

scenario: You want backups in a Recovery Services vault to be restorable in the paired region if the primary region is down. What should you configure, and when?

options.text: GRS and Cross Region Restore, before backups start
LRS with Cross Region Restore, at any time
options.note: CRR requires a GRS vault.

options.text: Copy the vault to another region manually.
options.note: Vaults can't be copied.
Soft delete protects against deletion, not regional outages.

explanation: A Recovery Services vault's storage redundancy (LRS, ZRS or GRS) can only be changed before you protect any items in it. Cross Region Restore requires GRS. Once it's enabled, you can restore backups in the paired secondary region at any time, including during an outage in the primary region.

refs.title: Restore VMs by using the Azure portal using Azure Backup: Cross Region Restore
Create and Configure Recovery Services Vaults

scenario: An attacker with admin access deletes backup data for several VMs. Which Azure Backup feature lets you recover the deleted backup data for a period after deletion?

options.text: Blob versioning on the vault's storage
options.note: Applies to storage accounts.
Protects the vault resource, not backup data inside it.
Doesn't recover deleted backups.

explanation: Soft delete for Azure Backup keeps deleted backup data for 14 days by default (configurable up to 180 days with enhanced soft delete), so you can undo a malicious or accidental deletion. Newly created vaults have soft delete on and it can't be turned off. Multi-user authorization and immutable vaults add more protection.

refs.title: Secure by Default with Soft Delete for Azure Backup

scenario: Before making changes to a VM, you start an on-demand backup. Where is the first recovery point stored for fast restores?

options.text: As a snapshot, then in the vault

options.note: Temporary disks aren't persistent.
Logs don't store data.
Stores logs, not backups.

explanation: A VM backup starts with a snapshot of the disks, kept for a short configurable period (instant restore). Restores from that snapshot are fast. The data then transfers to the vault for long-term retention, so the recovery point lives in both places for a while.

refs.title: Azure Instant Restore Capability

scenario: You need disaster recovery for Azure VMs in East US with replication to West US, a target RPO of minutes, and the ability to test failover without affecting production. What should you use?

options.text: Azure Backup with GRS and Cross Region Restore
options.note: Daily backups give an RPO of up to 24 hours, and restoring takes longer.
Unmanaged storage replication doesn't orchestrate VM failover.
Connectivity only.

explanation: Azure Site Recovery continuously replicates VMs to another region, with an RPO typically measured in minutes, and orchestrates failover and failback. A test failover creates VMs from replicated data in an isolated network, so you can prove disaster recovery works without touching production or stopping replication.

refs.title: Tutorial to set up Azure VM disaster recovery with Azure Site Recovery
About Azure Site Recovery

scenario: During a regional outage, multiple VMs must fail over in a specific order (database first, then app tier, then web tier) with a script between steps. What should you create in Site Recovery?

options.text: Three replication policies with different RPOs
options.note: Doesn't control order.
Unrelated.
Backup isn't failover.

explanation: A Site Recovery recovery plan groups VMs and fails the groups over in order, for example database, then app tier, then web tier. Between groups you can add manual actions or Azure Automation runbook scripts, which makes regional failover a repeatable process.

refs.title: About recovery plans in Azure Site Recovery

scenario: You restore a VM from backup and want to keep the original VM running for comparison. Which restore option should you choose?

options.note: Overwrites the original VM's disks.
Recovers individual files only.
Not a restore option.

explanation: Create new virtual machine builds a separate VM from the recovery point, so the original keeps running for comparison. Restore disks gives you disks to attach or build from a template, and Replace existing swaps the current VM's disks, so you'd lose the original state.

refs.title: Restore VMs by using the Azure portal using Azure Backup: Restore options

scenario: You need to see the pending OS updates for 200 Azure VMs and install critical updates every Saturday night. What should you use?

options.text: Azure Update Manager with a maintenance configuration

options.note: Retired with the Log Analytics agent; Update Manager replaces it.

options.text: The Custom Script Extension with a manual script
options.note: No assessment or compliance reporting.
Doesn't install patches.

explanation: Azure Update Manager assesses which updates are pending on Azure and Arc-enabled machines, with no extra agent. A maintenance configuration schedules installation, here critical updates every Saturday night, along with reboot behavior. Azure Automation Update Management was retired in August 2024.

refs.title: Azure Update Manager Overview

scenario: A VM-level alert should trigger an Azure Automation runbook that restarts a service. Where do you specify the runbook?

options.note: Severity is a label.
Defines collection only.

options.text: In the VM's boot diagnostics settings
options.note: Unrelated.

explanation: The alert rule decides when to fire, and the action group decides what happens. Action groups can run an Azure Automation runbook, a Function, a Logic App or a webhook, as well as send notifications. So you add the runbook that restarts the service as an action in the action group the alert uses.

refs.title: Create and manage action groups in Azure Monitor

scenario: Monitoring must capture an application's custom text log file (C:\App\logs\*.log) from VMs into Log Analytics. What should you configure?

options.text: A DCR with a custom text log data source
A diagnostic setting on the VM resource
options.note: Platform diagnostic settings don't read files inside the guest OS.
Console output only.

options.text: Network Watcher packet capture on the VM
options.note: Captures network traffic.

explanation: The Azure Monitor Agent can collect custom text and JSON log files through a data collection rule. The DCR sets the file path pattern (C:\App\logs\*.log), an optional transformation, and a custom table ending in _CL in the workspace. Diagnostic settings only cover platform and resource logs, not files inside the VM.

scenario: You enable self-service password reset (SSPR) for the group sspr-pilot and require two authentication methods. A Global Administrator in the pilot asks to use security questions as one of their methods. What happens?

options.text: Administrators can't use security questions; Microsoft Entra ID applies a stricter two-method policy to admin roles regardless of your SSPR settings.
Security questions work for admins if the tenant allows them for users.
options.note: Admin accounts follow the built-in two-gate policy, which excludes security questions.

options.text: Admins are excluded from SSPR and must call the help desk.
options.note: Admins have SSPR enabled by default; they just get a stricter policy.

options.text: The admin must be removed from sspr-pilot first.
options.note: Group scope applies to users; admin roles are always covered by their own policy.

explanation: Administrator roles always get a Microsoft-managed SSPR policy: two authentication methods, such as the Authenticator app, email or phone, and security questions are never allowed for admins. Your SSPR scope and method settings only apply to regular users, so the Global Administrator must pick other methods.

scenario: Users created in on-premises AD DS and synchronized with Microsoft Entra Connect reset their passwords with SSPR, but they still can't sign in to their domain-joined PCs with the new password. What must you configure?

options.text: Password writeback in Microsoft Entra Connect (and enable it in SSPR settings)

options.note: Registration affects who can use SSPR, not where the new password is stored.
The number of methods doesn't change where the password is written.
Seamless SSO uses the on-premises password; it doesn't send cloud resets back to AD DS.

explanation: Without password writeback, an SSPR reset changes only the cloud password, so domain-joined PCs, which authenticate against on-premises AD DS, still expect the old one. Turn on password writeback in Microsoft Entra Connect and in the SSPR settings so the new password is written back to AD DS. It requires Microsoft Entra ID P1 or higher.

scenario: Every member of the dynamic group Sales-All must receive a Microsoft 365 E3 license automatically, including people who join Sales later. What is the most efficient approach?

options.text: Assign the license to the Sales-All group (group-based licensing)
Assign the license to each user, and run a weekly script for new users
options.note: Works, but it's manual and misses users between runs.

options.text: Create an Azure Policy that assigns licenses
options.note: Azure Policy governs Azure resources, not Microsoft Entra licenses.

options.text: Add the license to the administrative unit that contains Sales
options.note: Administrative units delegate administration; they don't assign licenses.

explanation: Group-based licensing assigns a license to everyone in a group and adds or removes it automatically as membership changes. Assigning Microsoft 365 E3 to the dynamic group Sales-All means anyone who joins Sales later is licensed with no script or manual step.

scenario: All new resources must carry the costCenter tag of the resource group they're created in. Teams often forget to add it. What should you do?

options.text: Assign the built-in Azure Policy "Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing" and create a remediation task for existing resources
Add the tag to each resource group; resources inherit it automatically
options.note: Resources don't inherit tags from their resource group.

options.text: Apply a CanNotDelete lock to each resource group
options.note: Locks prevent deletion; they don't add tags.

options.text: Use a Deny policy that blocks resources without tags
options.note: That stops deployments instead of adding the tag; the requirement is to carry the value automatically.

explanation: Tags don't flow down from resource groups. The built-in policy Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing uses the Modify effect to copy the resource group's costCenter tag onto resources when they're created or updated. A remediation task applies it to resources that already exist.

scenario: Your organization wants to apply one Azure Policy to 40 subscriptions that belong to the finance department, and to any finance subscriptions created later. What should you use?

options.text: A management group that contains the finance subscriptions, with the policy assigned at that management group
A resource group in each subscription with the policy assigned there
options.note: Policy assigned to a resource group only covers that group.

options.text: A policy initiative assigned to each subscription individually
options.note: Initiatives group policies, but per-subscription assignment doesn't cover new subscriptions.

options.text: A tag on each subscription called department=finance
options.note: Tags don't carry policy assignments.

explanation: Put the finance subscriptions under one management group and assign the policy there. Policy and RBAC assignments at a management group are inherited by every subscription beneath it, including subscriptions moved in later, so there's one assignment to maintain instead of 40.

scenario: You gave a partner a service SAS URI for the container invoices. It was created from the stored access policy partner-read. The partner relationship has ended and access must stop immediately. What should you do?

options.text: Delete the stored access policy partner-read (or change its expiry to the past)
Delete the SAS URI from your records
options.note: The token stays valid; deleting your copy doesn't revoke it.
This also revokes access, but it breaks every other app and SAS that uses the keys.

options.text: Turn on soft delete for blobs
options.note: Soft delete protects data from deletion; it doesn't revoke access.

explanation: A service SAS created from a stored access policy gets its permissions and expiry from that policy on the server side. Deleting partner-read, or setting its expiry to the past, immediately invalidates every SAS linked to it, without touching the account keys. Regenerating keys would also break every other app that uses them.

scenario: A developer wants to issue a user delegation SAS for a blob and manage its expiry through a stored access policy. Why won't this work?

options.text: Stored access policies only apply to service SAS tokens, not to user delegation SAS or account SAS
User delegation SAS tokens can't be used with blobs
options.note: User delegation SAS is a blob-only SAS type.

options.text: Stored access policies are only for Azure Files
options.note: They work for containers, file shares, queues and tables.

options.text: A user delegation SAS can only last one hour
options.note: It can last up to seven days.

explanation: Stored access policies work only with service SAS tokens. A user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key obtained through Microsoft Entra ID, and an account SAS spans the whole account, so neither can reference a stored access policy. To revoke a user delegation SAS, revoke the delegation keys or the signer's permissions.

scenario: The storage account stlogs01 allows access only from selected networks. A Microsoft Fabric workspace must read data through its managed identity, and no other service of that type should get in. What should you configure?

options.text: A resource instance rule for that workspace in the storage account's networking settings
Enable "Allow Azure services on the trusted services list"
options.note: That admits trusted services broadly, not one specific instance.

options.text: Add the workspace's public IP addresses to the firewall
options.note: PaaS outbound IPs are shared and change; IP rules aren't meant for Azure services.
That removes the restriction for everyone.

explanation: A resource instance rule in the storage firewall allows one specific Azure resource, identified by its resource ID, through the network rules, here that Fabric workspace. Other instances of the same service stay blocked, unlike the broader trusted Microsoft services exception. The workspace's identity still needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader.

refs.title: Create a resource instance network rule for Azure Storage

scenario: You need blobs written to a container in steastprod (East US) to be copied automatically to a container in stwestdr (West US). Which settings must be in place?

options.text: Object replication, with blob versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source account
Geo-redundant storage (GRS) on the source account
options.note: GRS replicates the whole account to the paired region; you can't pick the target account or container.

options.text: A lifecycle management rule that copies new blobs
options.note: Lifecycle rules tier or delete blobs; they don't copy them.

options.text: Blob soft delete on both accounts
options.note: Soft delete isn't a prerequisite for object replication.

explanation: Object replication asynchronously copies block blobs from a container in one account to a container in another, which can be in a different region. It needs blob versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source account. GRS copies the whole account to a fixed paired region that you can't write to directly.

refs.title: Object replication overview

scenario: Two departments share a storage account. Finance data must be encrypted with a customer-managed key in Key Vault, while Marketing data uses Microsoft-managed keys. What should you use?

options.text: Encryption scopes, with a customer-managed-key scope set as the default on the finance container
A second storage account is the only option
options.note: That works too, but encryption scopes solve it within one account.

options.text: Infrastructure encryption on the finance container
options.note: Infrastructure encryption is enabled for a whole account, at creation, and adds a second layer; it doesn't pick keys per container.
That encrypts VM disks, not blob containers.

explanation: Encryption scopes let you choose the key per container or per blob within one storage account: a customer-managed key in Key Vault for Finance and Microsoft-managed keys for Marketing. Set the CMK scope as the finance container's default and enforce it, so every blob written there uses that key.

refs.title: Encryption scopes for Blob storage

scenario: A user deleted the file share projects in Azure Files four days ago. Soft delete for file shares was left at its default settings. What can you do?

options.text: Undelete the share from the storage account's File shares list (show deleted shares), because the default retention is 7 days
Nothing; deleted file shares can't be recovered
options.note: Share soft delete is on by default for new accounts.

options.text: Restore it from a blob version
options.note: Blob versioning doesn't cover Azure Files.

options.text: Open a support ticket to restore it from geo-redundant storage
options.note: GRS replicates deletions too; it isn't a backup.

explanation: Soft delete for Azure file shares is on by default with a 7-day retention period, so a share deleted four days ago can still be restored. In the storage account's File shares list, turn on Show deleted shares and choose Undelete. The share comes back with its snapshots.

refs.title: Azure File Share Soft Delete

scenario: An app uses key1 of a storage account in its connection string. Security requires rotating the account keys without downtime. In what order should you work?

options.text: Switch the app to key2, regenerate key1, then later switch back to key1 and regenerate key2
Regenerate both keys at the same time, then update the app
options.note: The app fails between the regeneration and the update.

options.text: Regenerate key1 first, then update the app
options.note: The app fails as soon as key1 changes.

options.text: Disable shared key access, then re-enable it
options.note: This doesn't rotate anything and blocks key-based access in the meantime.

explanation: Two access keys exist so you can rotate one while apps use the other. Move the app to key2, regenerate key1, and later move back to key1 and regenerate key2; the app never uses an invalid key. Even better, switch apps to Microsoft Entra authorization and disallow shared key access.

refs.title: Manage account access keys: Manually rotate access keys

scenario: An administrator signs in to Azure Storage Explorer with a Microsoft Entra account that has the Contributor role on the storage account, but gets "authorization permission mismatch" when listing blobs with Entra authentication. What is missing?

options.text: A data-plane role such as Storage Blob Data Reader or Storage Blob Data Contributor
The Owner role on the subscription
options.note: Owner manages resources but still doesn't grant blob data access through Entra ID.
A SAS is a different way to authorize; the question is about Entra authentication.

options.text: Public network access set to "Enabled from all networks"
options.note: A network block returns a different error; this is a permission problem.

explanation: Contributor is a control-plane role: it manages the storage account (and can read its keys), but it doesn't grant data access with Microsoft Entra ID. Listing blobs with Entra authorization needs a data-plane role such as Storage Blob Data Reader or Contributor. Role assignments can take a few minutes to apply.

Assign an Azure Role for Blob Data Access

scenario: You try to enable encryption at host on a new VM, but the option is unavailable. The VM size supports it. What should you check first?

options.text: That the EncryptionAtHost feature is registered for the Microsoft.Compute provider on the subscription
That Azure Disk Encryption is enabled first
options.note: It's the opposite: encryption at host can't be used on VMs that ever had Azure Disk Encryption.

options.text: That the VM uses an unmanaged disk
options.note: Encryption at host is for managed disks.

options.text: That the VM is in an availability set
options.note: Availability options are unrelated to this feature.

explanation: Encryption at host needs the EncryptionAtHost feature registered for the Microsoft.Compute resource provider on the subscription. Until it's registered, the option is unavailable even on supported VM sizes. Once on, temporary disks, disk caches and data flowing to storage are encrypted on the host.

refs.title: Enable end-to-end encryption using encryption at host

scenario: A VM has used Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) for years. Security now wants end-to-end encryption including the temporary disk and disk caches, using encryption at host. What is true?

options.text: Encryption at host can't be enabled on a VM that currently has or ever had ADE; you need a new VM with new disks
Enable encryption at host while the VM is running
options.note: Even without ADE, existing VMs must be deallocated first.

options.text: Encryption at host and ADE can be layered on the same VM
options.note: Microsoft blocks this combination.

options.text: Disable ADE, then enable encryption at host on the same VM
options.note: A VM that ever had ADE isn't eligible.

explanation: Encryption at host and Azure Disk Encryption can't be combined. A VM that has ADE enabled now, or ever had it, can't turn on encryption at host. To move to encryption at host, create a new VM with new disks and migrate the data.

refs.title: Server-side encryption of Azure managed disks: Encryption at host restrictions

scenario: You need to move a running VM, its disks and its network resources from East US to Sweden Central with a guided process that checks dependencies. What should you use?

options.text: Move the VM to another resource group
options.note: Moving between resource groups doesn't change its region.
Resizing changes the VM size, not its region.

options.text: Export the resource group template and edit the location
options.note: Possible but manual; it doesn't move disks or data.

explanation: Azure Resource Mover guides cross-region moves. It identifies dependencies such as disks, NICs, VNets and NSGs, validates them, and uses Azure Site Recovery replication to move the VM with minimal downtime. Moving between resource groups or subscriptions never changes the region.

refs.title: Move Azure VMs across regions with Azure Resource Mover

scenario: A container app must pull images from a private Azure Container Registry without storing a password. What is the recommended setup?

options.text: Give the container app a managed identity and assign it the AcrPull role on the registry
Enable the registry's admin user and store its password as a secret
options.note: This works, but it uses a shared password, which Microsoft discourages.
This exposes images to everyone.

options.text: Assign the container app the Contributor role on the registry
options.note: Contributor is far more than needed; AcrPull is the least-privilege role.

explanation: Give the container app a managed identity and assign it the AcrPull role on the registry. The app then pulls images with Microsoft Entra tokens, with no password stored anywhere. The ACR admin user is a shared credential that Microsoft recommends keeping disabled. Contributor would grant far more than pulling images.

refs.title: Azure Container Apps image pull from Azure Container Registry with managed identity
Azure Container Registry Entra permissions and role assignments overview

scenario: You want to send 10% of traffic to a new version of a container app and 90% to the current version, then shift traffic gradually. What must you configure?

options.text: Multiple revision mode, then set traffic weights on the two revisions
Single revision mode with two replicas
options.note: Single revision mode runs one active revision; replicas are copies of the same revision.

options.text: A second container app behind the same ingress
options.note: Container Apps does this natively with revisions.
Slots are an App Service feature, not Container Apps.

explanation: Each change to a container app's template creates a new revision. Switch the app to multiple revision mode so both revisions stay active, then set ingress traffic weights (10% new, 90% current) and shift them gradually. In single revision mode, only the latest revision receives traffic.

refs.title: Traffic splitting in Azure Container Apps

scenario: A nightly data job runs in Azure Container Instances. It should be restarted only if it exits with an error, and must stop after it succeeds. Which restart policy should you set?

options.note: The default; it restarts even after success, so the job would run endlessly.
It won't retry a failed run.
Not an ACI restart policy.

explanation: With restart policy OnFailure, Azure Container Instances restarts the container only when it exits with a non-zero (error) code. After a successful run, the container group stops and stops billing. Always would keep restarting a finished job, and Never wouldn't retry a failure.

refs.title: Restart policy for run-once tasks

scenario: You need to back up an App Service app every 2 hours, keep backups for 90 days, and store them in your own storage account. The app runs on a Standard plan. What should you configure?

options.text: A custom backup schedule that points to a storage account container
Automatic backups; they meet these requirements by default
options.note: Automatic backups are hourly with 30-day retention that you can't change.
Slots stage releases; they aren't backups.

options.text: Upgrade to Premium because Standard can't back up
options.note: Basic, Standard, Premium and Isolated all support backups.

explanation: App Service's automatic backups run hourly with 30-day retention, which doesn't meet the 90-day requirement. A custom backup lets you set your own schedule (every 2 hours) and retention (90 days), and writes to a storage account container you choose. Custom backups are available from the Basic tier and are limited to 10 GB.

refs.title: Back Up an App

scenario: You want to map www.contoso.com to an App Service app and secure it with a free certificate. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Add a CNAME record to the app's default host name and an asuid.www TXT record for verification, then create a free App Service managed certificate
A free managed certificate can cover *.contoso.com
options.note: Managed certificates don't support wildcard names.

options.text: Custom domains work on the Free (F1) tier with a managed certificate
options.note: Managed certificates and TLS bindings need a paid tier (Basic or higher).

options.text: Only an A record is needed, and the certificate is created automatically
options.note: A records are for root (apex) domains, and you must create the certificate and binding.

explanation: To add www.contoso.com, create a CNAME record pointing to the app's default host name, plus a TXT record named asuid.www with the app's domain verification ID. Then create a free App Service managed certificate. Managed certificates renew automatically but can't be wildcard or exported, and custom domains need Basic or higher.

refs.title: Set Up an Existing Custom Domain Name for Your App
Manage App Service Certificates

scenario: Before swapping a staging slot into production, you need the production slot to keep its own database connection string. What should you do?

options.text: Mark the connection string as a deployment slot setting in each slot
Store the connection string in the code
options.note: It would swap with the code.
Auto swap triggers swaps automatically; it doesn't keep settings in place.
Instance count doesn't affect which settings swap.

explanation: Marking the connection string as a deployment slot setting makes it "sticky": during a swap it stays with its slot instead of moving with the app. Mark it in each slot, so production keeps the production database and staging keeps the staging one after every swap.

refs.title: Set Up Staging Environments: Which settings are swapped

scenario: Your team has an ARM template JSON file and wants to maintain it in Bicep from now on. Which command creates a starting Bicep file?

options.note: build compiles Bicep into ARM JSON, the opposite direction.
Not a real conversion command; export works on existing resource groups.
az group create makes resource groups; it doesn't convert templates.

explanation: az bicep decompile --file main.json converts the ARM JSON template into a Bicep file as a starting point. It's best-effort, so review any warnings and tidy the generated names. az bicep build goes the other way, compiling Bicep into ARM JSON.

refs.title: Decompile a JSON Azure Resource Manager template to Bicep

scenario: You're creating a new scale set that must mix VM sizes and include Spot VMs, and you want to manage instances with standard VM operations. Which orchestration mode should you choose?

options.note: Uniform uses one identical VM model, which suits large stateless fleets.
Availability sets don't scale automatically.
It controls physical closeness, not orchestration.

explanation: Flexible orchestration manages instances as standard Azure VMs, so normal VM operations work on them. It supports mixing VM sizes and combining Spot with regular VMs in one scale set. Uniform mode uses identical instances of one size managed through the scale set model, and Microsoft recommends Flexible for new deployments.

refs.title: Orchestration modes for Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Azure

scenario: A VM's subnet has an NSG that allows inbound TCP 443 from the internet. The VM's NIC has another NSG with only the default rules. Can clients reach the VM on port 443?

options.text: No; inbound traffic must be allowed by both the subnet NSG and the NIC NSG, and the NIC's default rules deny it
Yes, because the subnet NSG is evaluated last and wins
options.note: For inbound traffic the subnet NSG is evaluated first, then the NIC NSG; both must allow it.

options.text: Yes, because NIC NSGs only filter outbound traffic
options.note: NSGs on NICs filter both directions.

options.text: Only if the VM has a Standard SKU public IP
options.note: The SKU doesn't override NSG rules.

explanation: For inbound traffic, Azure evaluates the subnet NSG and then the NIC NSG, and both must allow the traffic. The NIC NSG has only default rules, so its DenyAllInBound blocks port 443 even though the subnet NSG allows it. The NIC's Effective security rules view (on a running VM) shows the combined result.

refs.title: How Network Security Groups Filter Network Traffic in Azure

scenario: Admins must connect to VMs through Azure Bastion using the native SSH and RDP clients on their workstations (az network bastion ssh/rdp), not the browser. Which Bastion configuration supports this?

options.text: Standard or Premium SKU with native client support enabled

options.note: Developer is a free browser-only option for dev/test.
Basic doesn't support native client connections.

options.text: Any SKU, as long as the VMs have public IPs
options.note: Bastion exists so VMs don't need public IPs; native client needs Standard or higher.

explanation: Native client support, which lets you use az network bastion ssh and rdp from your workstation instead of the browser, requires the Standard or Premium SKU with Native client support turned on. The Developer and Basic SKUs only support browser connections.

refs.title: Configure Bastion for native client connections
Choose the right Azure Bastion SKU to meet your needs

scenario: Two backend VMs behind a Standard internal load balancer show as unhealthy, although the app responds locally on port 8080. The NSG has a custom rule DenyAllInbound at priority 4000. What is the likely cause?

options.text: The custom deny rule overrides the default AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound rule, so the health probe is blocked
Standard load balancers don't support health probes on port 8080
options.note: Probes can use any TCP or HTTP port.

options.text: The VMs need public IP addresses for probes
options.note: Probes come from the platform address 168.63.129.16, not over the internet.

options.text: Health probes only work with Basic load balancers
options.note: Basic load balancers were retired in 2025; Standard uses probes normally.

explanation: Health probes come from 168.63.129.16, which matches the AzureLoadBalancer service tag. The default rule that allows them, AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound, has priority 65001, so a custom DenyAllInbound at priority 4000 is evaluated first and blocks the probes. Add an allow rule for the AzureLoadBalancer tag with a number below 4000.

refs.title: Azure Load Balancer health probes: Probe source IP address
Azure network security groups overview: Default security rules

scenario: VMs in snet-app must reach a storage account over the Azure backbone. The storage account can keep its public endpoint, but only that subnet should be allowed, with no extra IP addresses to manage. What should you configure?

options.text: A Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on snet-app, plus a virtual network rule in the storage firewall
A private endpoint and a private DNS zone
options.note: Also secure, but it adds a private IP and DNS; a service endpoint meets the requirement more simply.

options.text: A NAT gateway on the subnet
options.note: It controls outbound internet IPs; it doesn't restrict the storage account to the subnet.

options.text: A user-defined route to the Internet next hop
options.note: Routing to Internet doesn't authorize the subnet at the storage firewall.

explanation: A Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on snet-app sends that subnet's storage traffic over the Azure backbone and identifies it to the service. A virtual network rule in the storage firewall then allows only that subnet, with no IP addresses to maintain. A private endpoint isn't needed because the account can keep its public endpoint.

refs.title: Create a virtual network rule for Azure Storage

scenario: You must back up Azure managed disks with incremental snapshots, and blobs with operational backup. Which vault type do you create?

options.note: Recovery Services vaults hold backups for VMs, Azure Files, SQL/SAP HANA in VMs and on-premises (MARS/MABS).
Key Vault stores secrets, keys and certificates, not backups.

options.text: A storage account with soft delete
options.note: Soft delete helps, but it isn't Azure Backup.

explanation: Azure Disk Backup (incremental snapshots) and operational backup for blobs are newer workloads that use a Backup vault. Recovery Services vaults serve Azure VMs, Azure Files and SQL or SAP HANA running inside VMs.

refs.title: Overview of Azure Disk Backup
Overview of the Backup vaults

scenario: Management wants weekly reports of backup jobs, storage used and policy compliance across 12 vaults. What must you configure first?

options.text: Diagnostic settings on each vault that send backup data to a Log Analytics workspace, then use Backup Reports
An action group with an email receiver
options.note: Action groups send alerts, not reports.

options.text: Cross Region Restore on each vault
options.note: It enables restores in the paired region; it doesn't produce reports.
Lifecycle policies tier or delete blobs; they don't report on backups.

explanation: Backup Reports query data in a Log Analytics workspace, so first add a diagnostic setting on each of the 12 vaults that sends backup data there, preferably in resource-specific mode. The reports then show jobs, storage used and policy compliance across every vault together.

refs.title: Configure Azure Backup reports

scenario: You replicate a production VM to another region with Azure Site Recovery. You must prove that failover works without affecting production or replication. What should you do?

options.text: Run a test failover into an isolated virtual network, then clean up the test failover
Run an unplanned failover to the production VNet
options.note: A real failover disrupts production.

options.text: Stop replication and restore from backup
options.note: This breaks protection and doesn't test Site Recovery.

options.text: Run a planned failover during business hours
options.note: A planned failover still moves production.

explanation: A test failover creates VMs from the replicated data in a network you choose, ideally isolated from production, while replication keeps running. Once you've confirmed the VMs work, run Cleanup test failover to delete the test resources. Production and replication are never affected.

refs.title: Tutorial to run an Azure VM disaster recovery drill with Azure Site Recovery

scenario: After a real Site Recovery failover to the secondary region, the VMs are running and confirmed healthy. What are the next steps to get protection and a way back?

options.text: Commit the failover, then re-protect the VMs so they replicate back to the primary region

options.note: You need them, or the primary region, for failback.
Testing doesn't restore replication.
This removes protection entirely.

explanation: Commit finalizes the failover and removes the other recovery points. Re-protect then starts replication in the opposite direction, from the secondary region back to the primary, so the VMs are protected again and you can later fail back with a planned failover.

refs.title: Tutorial to fail over Azure VMs to a secondary region for disaster recovery with Azure Site Recovery
Reprotect Azure virtual machines to the primary region with Azure Site Recovery

scenario: Every Saturday from 1 AM to 5 AM you patch servers, and alerts fire during the window. Alert rules should still evaluate, but no one should be notified then. What should you create?

options.text: An alert processing rule with a recurring schedule that suppresses notifications
Delete the alert rules and recreate them each week
options.note: Manual and error-prone.
You'd miss alerts outside the window too.

options.text: Raise the severity of the alerts
options.note: Severity doesn't stop notifications.

explanation: An alert processing rule with a recurring schedule (Saturdays 1 AM to 5 AM) suppresses the action groups of fired alerts during the window. Alert rules keep evaluating and alerts are still recorded, but no one gets notified. The same rules can also add action groups to many alert rules at once.

refs.title: Alert processing rules for Azure Monitor alerts

scenario: You need to continuously measure reachability, latency and packet loss between Azure VMs and an on-premises server, and be alerted when it degrades. Which tool fits?

options.text: Connection monitor in Azure Network Watcher

options.note: IP flow verify tests one packet against NSG rules at a point in time.
It shows the next routing hop, not ongoing performance.
Flow logs record traffic; they don't measure latency between endpoints.

explanation: Connection monitor in Network Watcher runs scheduled tests between Azure VMs or scale sets and on-premises machines (through Azure Arc and the Azure Monitor Agent) or URLs. It continuously records reachability, round-trip time and packet loss, and alerts when they degrade. IP flow verify and Next hop are one-off checks.

refs.title: Connection Monitor Overview

scenario: You need VM insights performance charts and the dependency map for 30 VMs. What do the VMs need?

options.text: The Azure Monitor Agent with a VM insights data collection rule (and the Dependency agent for the map)

options.note: Boot diagnostics captures console screenshots and logs only.
MMA was retired in August 2024.

options.text: Network Watcher enabled in the region
options.note: Network Watcher doesn't collect guest performance data.

explanation: VM insights collects guest performance data through the Azure Monitor Agent and a VM insights data collection rule that sends it to Log Analytics. The Map feature also needs the Dependency agent. You can enable it from Monitor > Insights > Virtual machines, or for all 30 VMs at once with Azure Policy.

refs.title: Enable VM monitoring in Azure Monitor
